cells.tense: You can end a thing fully when it is time and not a moment before.
cells.ask: Name one thing you are already done with, say out loud that it is finished, and let the next day pass without reopening it.
cells.core:
Something ends, and you let it end — all the way, the way you close a book rather than leave it face-down on the table. You are not rushing the finish and not holding it open past its time. That is the whole of it: an ending recognized, and what comes after it met without a fight.

What this gives you is clean hands. Nothing is half-finished in the background pulling at you while you are trying to do something else, and the fair exchange between you and the people around you has room to move. The cost of keeping it is attention — checking back on what is closed. Your next step is small: pick one finished thing and let it stay finished.
cells.sheetLine: You can end a thing fully, and you do.
cells.verb: let what has already ended finish, and trust what follows it
cells.place: at the point where you finally open your hands and let the thing go

cells.tense: You are cutting things loose ahead of the moment they are actually finished.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you have been about to end and leave it alone for a week — no announcement, no quiet withdrawal — then see what it looks like.
cells.core:
Every ending is arriving early. Something has barely started and already you are rehearsing the goodbye, cleaning out the room before anyone has moved in. It feels like freedom. It reads more like getting out ahead of something you would rather not sit through.

Endings you control are easier than endings that happen to you, so you keep making them. What that costs is anything that needs time to grow. The release you are after is real, it is just aimed wrong — pointed at what is still alive instead of at what has actually run its course. Let one thing be unfinished this week and notice what the waiting stirs up.
cells.sheetLine: You keep ending things before they have had a chance.
cells.verb: let what has already ended finish, and trust what follows it
cells.place: at the point where you finally open your hands and let the thing go

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that has already closed, still holding it the way it was.
cells.ask: Take one object, note, or saved message that belongs to something over, delete it or box it, and do not tell anyone you did.
cells.core:
Something is over and you have not moved from it. Not because you are confused about it — because moving can look like turning on what it was. So you stay, keeping the shape of it intact, and nothing new gets the room it needs. Staying looks like loyalty from where you are standing.

The thing you are guarding is not being kept alive by this. It is just being kept present, and it costs you the space where something else would go. Letting go does not erase what it was; it stops asking it to keep standing in for a life. One small clearing, done quietly, is enough to start.
cells.sheetLine: You are holding a door closed that already closed itself.
cells.verb: let what has already ended finish, and trust what follows it
cells.place: at the point where you finally open your hands and let the thing go

cells.tense: Something in you is already ending and you have not noticed it ending.
cells.ask: Write down three things you did this week out of habit, look at the list, and say which one you would not choose again.
cells.core:
There is an ending in progress and you are not in the room for it. Your life has already rearranged itself — what you reach for, what you no longer bother with — and you are still describing it the old way, as if nothing had changed. The clearing is happening. Nobody has said so.

Naming it does not cause the loss; it just lets you take part in it instead of being done to. Things get clear, which is what you are good at once you decide to be, and what is actually over stops quietly keeping you busy. Write the three lines down and read them back.
cells.sheetLine: Something has already ended and you have not said so.
cells.verb: let what has already ended finish, and trust what follows it
cells.place: at the point where you finally open your hands and let the thing go

The claim it does not support is anything about what has actually ended in this person's life, so no cell locates an ending, a relationship, a job, or a time. A reader could reasonably say the too-much cell reads like restlessness rather than fear, and the too-little cell like plain loyalty — both are written so that 'that's not it' still leaves something usable. The asks do not depend on the read being right: each one is a small act that stands on its own whether or not the diagnosis lands. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'fear disguised as liberation' — it sounds sharp and tells the person nothing, so it is kept out of the cells entirely.
